{{short description|Graph made from vertices and edges of a convex polyhedron}}
[[File:Dodecahedron schlegel.svg|thumb|The polyhedral graph formed as the [[Schlegel diagram]] of a [[regular dodecahedron]].]]
In [[geometric graph theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a '''polyhedral graph''' is the [[undirected graph]] formed from the [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] and [[Edge (geometry)|edges]] of a [[convex polyhedron]]. Alternatively, in purely graph-theoretic terms, the polyhedral graphs are the [[k-vertex-connected graph|3-vertex-connected]], [[planar graph]]s. The analogue concept for [[Polytope|polytopes]] of general dimension are the [[Graph of a polytope|polytopal graphs]].

==Characterization==
The [[Schlegel diagram]] of a convex polyhedron represents its vertices and edges as points and line segments in the [[Euclidean plane]], forming a subdivision of an outer [[convex polygon]] into smaller convex polygons (a [[convex drawing]] of the graph of the polyhedron). It has no crossings, so every polyhedral graph is also a [[planar graph]]. Additionally, by [[Balinski's theorem]], it is a [[k-vertex-connected graph|3-vertex-connected graph]].

According to [[Steinitz's theorem]], these two graph-theoretic properties are enough to completely [[Characterization (mathematics)|characterize]] the polyhedral graphs: they are exactly the 3-vertex-connected planar graphs. That is, whenever a graph is both planar and 3-vertex-connected, there exists a polyhedron whose vertices and edges form an [[graph isomorphism|isomorphic]] graph.<ref>{{citation|title=Lectures on Polytopes|first=Günter M.|last=Ziegler|author-link=Günter M. Ziegler|year=1995|isbn=0-387-94365-X|chapter=Chapter 4: Steinitz' Theorem for 3-Polytopes|pages=103–126|publisher=Springer }}</ref><ref name=grun>{{citation|first=Branko|last=Grünbaum|authorlink=Branko Grünbaum|title=Convex Polytopes|title-link=Convex Polytopes|edition=2nd|year=2003|isbn=978-0-387-40409-7|publisher=Springer-Verlag|series=[[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]]|volume=221}}.</ref> Given such a graph, a representation of it as a subdivision of a convex polygon into smaller convex polygons may be found using the [[Tutte embedding]].<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Tutte | first = W. T. | authorlink = W. T. Tutte
 | title = How to draw a graph
 | journal = Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society
 | volume = 13
 | year = 1963
 | issue = 1 | pages = 743–767
 | mr = 0158387
 | doi = 10.1112/plms/s3-13.1.743 | bibcode = 1963PLMS...13..743T }}.</ref>

==Hamiltonicity and shortness==
[[Tait's conjecture|Tait conjectured]] that every [[cubic graph|cubic]] polyhedral graph (that is, a polyhedral graph in which each vertex is incident to exactly three edges) has a [[Hamiltonian cycle]], but this conjecture was disproved by a [[counterexample]] of [[W. T. Tutte]], the polyhedral but non-[[Hamiltonian graph|Hamiltonian]] [[Tutte graph]]. If one relaxes the requirement that the graph be cubic, there are much smaller non-Hamiltonian polyhedral graphs. The graph with the fewest vertices and edges is the 11-vertex and 18-edge [[Herschel graph]],<ref>{{citation|title=Hamiltonian circuits on 3-polytopes|first1=David|last1=Barnette|first2=Ernest|last2=Jucovič|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]|volume=9|issue=1|year=1970|pages=54–59|doi=10.1016/S0021-9800(70)80054-0|doi-access=free}}</ref> and there also exists an 11-vertex non-Hamiltonian polyhedral graph in which all faces are triangles, the [[Goldner–Harary graph]].<ref>{{citation|first1=A.|last1=Goldner|first2=F.|last2=Harary|author2-link=Frank Harary|title=Note on a smallest nonhamiltonian maximal planar graph|journal=Bull. Malaysian Math. Soc.|volume=6|issue=1|year=1975|pages=41–42}}</ref>

More strongly, there exists a constant <math>\alpha<1</math> (the [[shortness exponent]]) and an infinite family of polyhedral graphs such that the length of the longest [[path (graph theory)|simple path]] of an <math>n</math>-vertex graph in the family is <math>O(n^{\alpha})</math>.<ref>{{citation|title=Longest simple paths in polyhedral graphs|first1=Branko|last1=Grünbaum|author1-link=Branko Grünbaum|first2=T. S.|last2=Motzkin|journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society|year=1962|volume=s1-37|issue=1|pages=152–160|doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-37.1.152}}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Owens | first = Peter J.
 | doi = 10.1016/S0012-365X(98)00402-6
 | issue = 1–3
 | journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1665396
 | pages = 159–169
 | title = Shortness parameters for polyhedral graphs
 | volume = 206
 | year = 1999| doi-access = 
 }}</ref>

A problem with one additional constraint exists, [[Barnette's conjecture]], asking whether every cubic ''[[bipartite graph|bipartite]]'' polyhedral graph is Hamiltonian, which remains unsolved.

==Combinatorial enumeration==
Duijvestijn provides a count of the polyhedral graphs with up to 26 edges;<ref>{{citation|title=The number of polyhedral (3-connected planar) graphs|first=A. J. W.|last=Duijvestijn|journal=Mathematics of Computation|volume=65|year=1996|issue=215 |pages=1289–1293|doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-96-00749-1|url=https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/files/7051864/number_of_plyhedral.pdf|doi-access=free}}.</ref> The number of these graphs with 6, 7, 8, ... edges is
:1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 4, 12, 22, 58, 158, 448, 1342, 4199, 13384, 43708, 144810, ... {{OEIS|A002840}}.
One may also [[graph enumeration|enumerate]] the polyhedral graphs by their numbers of vertices: for graphs with 4, 5, 6, ... vertices, the number of polyhedral graphs is
:1, 2, 7, 34, 257, 2606, 32300, 440564, 6384634, 96262938, 1496225352, ... {{OEIS|A000944}}.

==Special cases==
{{Hamiltonian_platonic_graphs.svg|240px}}
The [[Graph of a polytope|vertex-edge graphs]] of the [[Platonic solid]]s are also called ''Platonic graphs''. As well as having all the other properties of polyhedral graphs, these are [[symmetric graph]]s, and all of them have [[Hamiltonian cycle]]s.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Read | first1 = Ronald C.
 | last2 = Wilson | first2 = Robin J. |author-link2=Robin Wilson (mathematician)
 | chapter = Chapter 6: Special graphs
 | isbn = 0-19-853289-X
 | mr = 1692656
 | pages = 261, 266
 | publisher = Oxford University Press
 | series = Oxford Science Publications
 | title = An Atlas of Graphs
 | year = 1998}}</ref> There are five of these graphs:

* [[Tetrahedral graph]] – 4 vertices, 6 edges
* [[Octahedral graph]] – 6 vertices, 12 edges
* [[Cubical graph]] – 8 vertices, 12 edges
* [[Icosahedral graph]] – 12 vertices, 30 edges
* [[Dodecahedral graph]] – 20 vertices, 30 edges

A polyhedral graph is the graph of a [[simple polyhedron]] if it is [[cubic graph|cubic]] (every vertex has three edges), and it is the graph of a [[simplicial polyhedron]] if it is a [[maximal planar graph]]. For example, the tetrahedral, cubical, and dodecahedral graphs are simple; the tetrahedral, octahedral, and icosahedral graphs are simplicial.

The [[Halin graph]]s, graphs formed from a planar embedded [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] by adding an outer cycle connecting all of the leaves of the tree, form another important subclass of the polyhedral graphs.
